title: A blind Gaia DR3 and ZTF search of 1,276 high-scatter field dwarfs recovers Gaia20cdd and finds four new aperiodic dimmers; UV and Gaia XP data exclude a nova-like origin for Gaia20cdd
abstract: Gaia20cdd is an old thick-disc K-type star with deep, irregular dips. Prior campaign work attributed them to small dust grains and found a 4.6 um excess. We asked whether a blind survey finds similar stars and whether other causes explain Gaia20cdd. We selected Gaia DR3 stars with G < 18, |b| > 20 deg and a G-band epoch scatter above 10 percent (29,042 stars, the top 0.1 percent), kept 1,998 unclassified main-sequence dwarfs, and searched ZTF DR24 light curves of 1,276 of them for dimming over at least 3 consecutive nights. Gaia20cdd is the deepest event (3.4 mag), a positive control. Of 40 passes, 31 are eclipsing or contact binaries and 5 are aperiodic dimmers: Gaia20cdd and four stars that SIMBAD does not list. One new M dwarf (Gaia DR3 3768075658908734720, 510 pc) faded by 0.4-0.7 mag in 2018 and recovered by 2020; it has a W1-W2 excess (redder than all 586 controls) and W1-W3 = 2.7 mag. Two of four dimmers with WISE data have a W1-W2 excess that 3.5 percent of high-scatter dwarfs have (binomial p = 0.007), but only one survives a strict contamination cut (p = 0.10). VSX lists Gaia20cdd as a possible VY Scl nova-like. GALEX gives NUV = 22.79 +- 0.31, 7 mag fainter than a disc that gives the optical flux; Gaia XP shows H-alpha absorption; Pan-STARRS1 shows no flickering; the colours are those of a K star. Thus the K star itself is occulted. Legacy Survey forced photometry, which models the neighbours, gives W1-W2 = 0.171 +- 0.012 against a field median of -0.059 (0 of 37 redder), so the warm excess is not a blend. Mie radiation pressure blows out the fitted silicate grains only if L > about 0.3 L_sun. Limitations: the search is incomplete and has no injection test; vetting is visual; the infrared association rests on one or two stars; no spectra.
